Five numbered sections plus untitled introduction: §1 Perceiving time; §2 Measuring time; §3 Memory, imagination, the perception of time, and the perception of motion; §4 The effect of intellect on the perception of time; §5 Physics 4.14: if there were no nous would there be time?
44 footnotes with substantial scholarly apparatus (full survey of the controversy on Aristotle's mathematical objects in fn. 7, citing White 1993 and Mignucci 1987)
Three primary ancient commentators introduced as anchors: Albert the Great (B. Alberti Magni 1890, p. 100) §1, Themistius (1899, 120.12-17) §1, Pseudo-Philoponus (Philoponus 1897, 580.27-37) §4

Engages prior cluster authors: Sorabji 1983, 1993, 2004 cited eight times (his time-perception interpretation rejected on the 'perceiving as a broader sense' point at fn. 25); Coope 2005 cited as foil for the 'counting brings nows into existence' line (fn. 12, 18, 42); Cashdollar 1973 cited on incidental perception (fn. 15); Caston 1996 cited approvingly on incidental perception (fn. 16, 31)

Resolution of the memory–time-perception circularity routed entirely through De Memoria 1, 450a19-22 + De Memoria 2, 452b31-453a4 (the two-phantasmata account)

Bibliography is comprehensive of the modern debate (Ackrill, Beare, Block, Cashdollar, Caston, Charlton, Coope, Gregoric, Hamlyn, Hussey, Irwin, James, Kahn, King, Magnus, McKirahan, Mignucci, Moss, Nieder, Philoponus, Polansky, Quine, Sorabji, Taormina, Themistius, Todd, Tye, White, Ziolkowski)

section_structure.heading: [Introduction — untitled opening, sets the perceiving-vs-cognizing distinction]
section_structure.summary: Bowin opens by aggregating Aristotle's claims that time can be perceived (Phys. 4.11.219a3-4 perceiving motion and time together; Phys. 4.11.219a30-b1 perceiving instants/nows) and that time can be grasped intellectually (De Memoria 1, 449b29, 450a19, 451a17 perception-of-time-in-remembering; De Memoria 2, 452b7 'apprehending time by a measure'). The chapter's two-pronged thesis is announced: (i) perceiving time does not presuppose grasping it intellectually — this protects animal sagacity (Meta. Α.1, 980a28 ff. crediting animals with memory, which in turn presupposes recognizing that we learned something before, Mem. 1.450a14-450a20), and (ii) grasping time intellectually nonetheless has an effect on how rational beings perceive it. Two challenges are entertained: (a) Aristotle's definition of time as a 'number of motion in respect of the before and after' (Phys. 4.11.219b1-2) might appear to require counting and so intellect; (b) Physics 4.14 'no soul, no time' might appear to make time mind-dependent. Both are deferred to §§2 and 5.

section_structure.heading: 1. Perceiving time
section_structure.summary: The longest single section. Bowin works through three ancient/medieval commentators (Albert the Great, Themistius, Pseudo-Philoponus) whose readings over-mathematize Physics 4.11. Albert the Great's twofold-time-perception thesis (Alberti Magni 1890, p. 100) treats rational beings as the only perceivers of time in itself, animals as relational time-perceivers — Bowin rejects on the ground that 'number' in the definition refers to instantaneous stages of motion, not to the act of counting. Themistius (1899, 120.12-17) takes perceiving time as requiring nous and arithmein — also rejected. Bowin argues that mathematical objects for Aristotle are sensible objects studied qua having certain properties (citing Metaph. B.2.997b35-998a6; K.1.1059b10-12; Θ.1.1051a21-33; M.3.1078a28-31, with the controversy surveyed at fn. 7 via White 1993 and Mignucci 1987). Crucially: instantaneous motion stages are perfectly and actually indivisible qua instantaneous; no abstraction is required to bring them to actuality. So perceiving time CAN be perceiving a number of nows directly. The Physics 4.11.219a22-a29 'soul says the nows are two' passage is parsed: 'number' here means a plurality of instantaneous motion stages bounded by a now-before and a now-after, with temporal duration lying between. Bowin rebuts the Coope/Sorabji-type reading that nows are brought into existence by the act of counting (fn. 12 to Coope; fn. 18 to Coope and Sorabji 1983 p. 84 ff.): nows have potential existence ('the now divides potentially,' Phys. 4.13.222a14), Physics 8.8.263a27-8, 263b3-6 has infinitely many potential parts of time, so nows already exist prior to counting. Even granted nows must be marked off to exist, marking off can be discrimination, and perception discriminates (Post. An. 2.19.99b35; Top. 2.4.111a14-20; DA 2.11.424a6; DA 3.2.426b8-21). Two evidential moves: (i) Aristotle credits non-rational animals with perception of individual phantasmata (DA 2.12.424a19 signet-ring metaphor; Mem. 1.450a27-32 mechanical metaphor; Mem. 2.452b23 ff. the time-lapse phantasma; Mem. 1.449b31-450a7 phantasmata as raw material for the intellect's grasp of essences). Phantasmata appear AS, indeed ARE, fully individuated particulars in the De Memoria. (ii) The common sense in animals perceives number directly (DA 3.1, 425a16; DA 2.6.418a7-11): just as it perceives 'two' or 'three' of any sensible item without counting (Aristotle credits this in HA 6.6 with the eagle laying three eggs and hatching two). The verb arithmein appears 8 times after the definition at 219b1-2 in the remainder of Book 4 (three times concerned with counting only, three times repeating the count-vs-countable distinction, two idiosyncratic uses — fn. 19) — counting plays a much smaller role than commentators have supposed. Conclusion: perceiving the nows are two (or three or four), and their order of succession, requires only the common sense; it discriminates the number and relative magnitude of motion stages.

section_structure.heading: 2. Measuring time
section_structure.summary: The pivot from perceiving to measuring. Bowin defines measuring time as 'either perceiving a number (two or more) of nows, or perceiving how much time has passed, in purely relative terms, by perceiving the order as well as the number of nows.' Perceiving time requires no counting. Measuring time DOES require counting and therefore nous. The verb arithmein at Phys. 4.14.223b13-24 is used in an extended sense to mean measuring: 'time too by some determinate (hōrismenon) time, and since, as we said, time is measured by motion and motion by time… uniform circular motion is most of all a measure.' Counting is the type of measurement most exact because absolutely indivisible in relation to perception (Metaph. I.1.1053a1, 23). Continua such as durations can only have 'a number of a sort' (Phys. 4.12.220a27-8) — divided into parts. It is in this extended sense, in measurement, that the process of counting has any prominence in chapters Phys. 4.10-14. Measuring time affords an intellectual grasp (gnōrizein) of time as De Memoria 2, 452b8-9 and 452b30-453a4 explicitly say — '…apprehend (gnōrizein) the time, either by a measure (metrō) or indeterminately (aoristōs).' Bowin reads the Mem. passage as preserving the apprehension-vs-perception (gnōrizein vs aisthanesthai) and the cognition-vs-perception (dianoeisthai vs aisthanesthai) contrasts (cf. GA 1.23.731a33-4). The genus-of-measure constraint requires sortal concepts (day, hour) that animals lack; thus measuring time is achievement of intellect. Apprehending time INDETERMINATELY, on the other hand, is achievement of perception: merely perceiving that time has passed since a remembered event, but not knowing how much.

section_structure.heading: 3. Memory, imagination, the perception of time, and the perception of motion
section_structure.summary: The chapter's most philosophically dense section. Bowin distinguishes perceiving-time-as-it-is-passing from perceiving-that-time-has-passed (perceiving its passage). He argues Aristotle is concerned only with the latter — in Physics 4.11 Aristotle speaks of perceiving time having passed (gegonenai chronos, perfect tense), not perceiving time passing. The puzzle of the ceasing instant (Phys. 4.10.218a8-21) and the always-other-and-other now (Phys. 4.11.219b9-10) are references to temporal passage but not to perceiving time passing. So Bowin reads De Memoria 1's perception-of-time as perceiving-that-time-has-elapsed-since-a-remembered-event, NOT distinguishing it from perceiving-time-as-passing. Two reasons: first, perceiving time as passing is not Aristotle's topic; second, perceiving time having passed reduces to perceiving that a remembered event is distinct from what one is now experiencing. The relationship between memory and the perception of motion: to perceive motion is to perceive a plurality of motion stages, and since only one instantaneous motion stage can be present at a time, some past motion stages will need to be remembered. Hence both the perception of time AND the perception of motion seem to presuppose memory. But memory itself requires the perception of time (Mem. 1.449b28-29). So memory and the perception of time appear to presuppose each other. Bowin's resolution: the De Memoria 1, 450a19-22 passage — 'When someone is actively engaged in memory, he perceives in addition (prosaisthanetai) that he saw this, or heard it, or learned it before; and before and after are in time.' Chapter 2 explains: both memory and the perception of time involve PHANTASMATA — two phantasmata, one representing the event remembered and one representing the time elapsed (Mem. 2.452b31-453a4). To remember, one must have a phantasma of an event happened before to MATCH a phantasma of a movement corresponding to the event. If either is missing, one fails to remember. Hence memory presupposes the perception of time, and both presuppose having phantasmata, but the perception of time does NOT presuppose memory. The perception of time depends on PHANTASIA (footnote 29 at Mem. 1.450a9-11 corroborates). Bowin entertains and dismisses Sorabji's regress worry: that the phantasma of the event corresponding to the time would itself require a further series of phantasmata. Bowin's reply: 'to perceive time and to remember an event is the same activity under different descriptions' — to perceive time is to perceive a number of events ordered as before and after, and to perceive a phantasma of an event that happened before AS before must inevitably be a phantasma. The circularity is interdefinitional, not vicious. To round out the parallel for motion: a retained plurality of phantasmata represents motion stages, but they need not be perceived AS having happened before. If past motion phases are represented by phantasmata not perceived as before, then perceiving a number of motion stages is not sufficient for perceiving time. Bowin gestures toward a 'specious present' reading (James 1905 vol. 1 p. 631; Sorabji 2004 p. 91 detects this at Mem. 1.451a31) but notes there is little evidence for this concept in Aristotle.

section_structure.heading: 4. The effect of intellect on the perception of time
section_structure.summary: Pseudo-Philoponus (Philoponus 1897, 580.27-37; Charlton 2000 p. 31) is the anchor: by 'time' Aristotle means determinate (hōrismenon) time, not indeterminate (aoriston) time; this distinguishes from de Interpretatione's 'some simply, some in time' (de Int. 1, 16a18, with Ackrill 1963 p. 115 and Charlton 2000 p. 64 n. 30 read against Bowin's gloss). Non-rational beings, even if they have synaisthēsis of time, do not have conscious perception of determinate time but only of indeterminate seasons. Humans alone perceive determinate time because they count days and hours; counting is proper to the rational soul (logikē psychē). The distinction is between TYPES OF PERCEPTION (aisthēsis), not apprehension in general (gnōsis). Determinate time is a time used as a measure because marked out by regular motion (Phys. 4.14). Pseudo-Philoponus is commenting on De Anima 3.10, 433b5-11 (conflict between reason and desire requires perception of time in beings where logos and epithumiai are present). The perception of time relevant in DA 3.10 is not the kind in Phys. 4.10-14 or De Memoria — it amounts to perceiving an ordered series of past or present events, perceiving the future. Aristotle holds we do not perceive the future strictly (Mem. 1, 449b27, fn. 35 with Taormina 2002 dissent), but we can perceive phantasmata that are LIKE perceiving the future (DA 3.7.431b6-8: 'sometimes by means of the phantasmata or thoughts which are within the soul, just as if it were seeing, [the faculty of thinking] calculates and deliberates what is to come'). This involves DELIBERATION — and so DELIBERATIVE PHANTASIA (DA 3.11.434a6-15), contrasted with perceptual phantasia, which is found in calculating beings and 'pursues one image greater out of many phantasmata'. Bowin reads Plato Protagoras 356d-e's metrētikē technē as the model: deliberative phantasia synthesizes phantasmata into a unified phantasma we use to reckon time — days, months, years. This supports Pseudo-Philoponus's distinction: determinate-time perception is a function of deliberative phantasia (modified by intellect); indeterminate-time perception is a function of perceptual phantasia. Bowin grounds the synthesis-of-images thesis in Posterior Analytics 2.19.100a3-9 (memory–experience–universal) and Metaphysics Α.1.980b26-981a12 ('many memories of the same thing produce finally the capacity for a single experience'); deliberative phantasia is the analog of empeiria-formation but with active intellectual manipulation. The Polansky 2007 p. 530 and Moss 2012 p. 146 reading (deliberative phantasia distinguished only by use) is contested at fn. 37: Bowin insists on a phenomenal-content difference. Closing worry addressed: does conceptual content thereby contaminate perception? Bowin's reply (fn. 39, with Tye 1995 pp. 140-141 cited): the normalized image of a day, shorn of its rough seasonal variations, can be non-conceptual perceptual content even if a sortal concept guided its production. The Posterior Analytics 2.19.100a6-7 'or from the whole universal that has come to rest in the soul' is read epexegetically following Sorabji 1993 p. 34 (fn. 40). Empeiria in animals may be non-conceptual (NE 7.3.1147b5 animals have no universal beliefs but only imagination and memory of particulars), supporting the layered model.

section_structure.heading: 5. Physics 4.14: if there were no nous would there be time?
section_structure.summary: The Physics 4.14.223a21-29 passage: 'if it is impossible that there should be something to do the counting, it is also impossible that anything should be countable… But if there is nothing that has it in its nature to count except soul… it is impossible that there should be time if there is no soul, except that there could be what underlies time; as for example if it is possible for there to be motion without soul. The before and after are in motion, and time is these qua countable.' Naively this seems to make time depend on counting and hence intellect, threatening Bowin's main thesis. Bowin's resolution: the perception of time would depend counterfactually only on the existence of beings who can count, which does not require beings who perceive time to be able to count. In fact, perceiving time, or before-and-after in motion qua countable, does not require beings who perceive time as countable. Still, what is the mind-dependence of time implied here? Many commentators (Mignucci 1987 pp. 184-186; fn. 43) treat this as a straightforward logical error or modality confusion (Sorabji 1983 p. 89 ff.). Bowin's positive reading: in the absence of beings with nous, time would not be MEASURABLE (or countable in the extended sense), but motion's before-and-after would still obtain. He grounds this in Metaph. Δ.15 (measurables/knowables/visibles are relatives but called such not because they are of something else but because something else, that is, a measure or knowledge, is of them); Categories 7.6b28-36 (the measurable is measurable BY the measure, instrumental dative). The measure is only incidentally related to the measurable's measurability. Then for plurality measure is always automatic (every horse in the plurality, etc.); for continua such as time and motion the measure is only by appearance as indivisible (Metaph. I.1.1053a1, 23). The deliberative-phantasia-produced normalized phantasma of a day is an 'inner movement' or phantasma; without nous and hence without deliberative phantasia, time would not be measurable because no measure would stand in a measuring relation to it, nor would it be countable in the extended sense of time being countable by means of some determinate time. The 'no soul, no time' passage collapses into the modest claim: no soul, no determinate measure of time.

outline: Bowin's chapter is structured around a single load-bearing distinction: PERCEIVING time vs INTELLECTUALLY GRASPING time. The introduction announces the two-pronged thesis — (i) perceiving time does not presuppose intellectual grasp, (ii) intellectual grasp affects how rational beings perceive time — and previews the two interpretive obstacles (the 'number of motion' definition; Phys. 4.14 'no soul, no time'). Section 1 establishes (i) negatively against the ancient commentators (Albert the Great, Themistius) who over-mathematize Phys. 4.11. It works through three sub-arguments: (a) mathematical objects for Aristotle do not require abstraction in the time case because instantaneous motion stages are actually indivisible; (b) the 'soul says the nows are two' passage is about perceiving, not counting, nows — the common sense perceives number directly; (c) the verb arithmein is reserved for counting-as-measuring and appears AFTER the definition at 219b1-2. Section 2 distinguishes perceiving time (no counting) from measuring time (counting, hence nous), routing the distinction through Mem. 2.452b8-9 (gnōrizein vs aisthanesthai). Section 3 confronts the apparent circularity: memory presupposes perception of time (Mem. 1.449b28-29), and perception of time/motion presupposes memory (because past motion stages must be remembered). The resolution invokes Mem. 1.450a19-22 (the prosaisthanetai passage) and Mem. 2.452b31-453a4 (the two-phantasmata account): both memory and time-perception are mediated by phantasmata, but the perception of time does not presuppose memory — perceiving a phantasma of a past event AS past is itself constitutive of perceiving time. The circularity is interdefinitional, non-vicious. Section 4 turns to thesis (ii): how intellect modulates perception of time. Pseudo-Philoponus's determinate/indeterminate-time distinction is appropriated. Determinate-time perception is a function of deliberative phantasia (DA 3.11.434a6-15), which synthesizes phantasmata into a unified day/month/year phantasma usable as a measure; indeterminate-time perception is a function of perceptual phantasia and is available to animals. Section 5 defuses the Phys. 4.14 passage: 'no soul, no time' is not the claim that time depends on counting, but that time would not be MEASURABLE without nous; motion's before-and-after still obtains. The chapter closes with a Metaph. Δ.15 and Cats. 7 analysis of the measurable-by-measure instrumental relation. The argumentative architecture is therefore tripartite: (§1) defend the perception-of-time-without-intellect thesis exegetically; (§§2-4) deliver the positive account of how intellect modulates perception through deliberative phantasia; (§5) defuse the most threatening counterexample. The chapter's deepest contribution is the routing of the memory–time-perception circularity through phantasmata at Mem. 1.450a19-22 — which is exactly the doctrinal site at which this chapter bridges into the Aristotelian Phantasia Secondary pipeline.

concepts.label: Perception of time
concepts.summary: The non-intellectual capacity to perceive a number of nows ordered as before-and-after — available to all animals with perceptual phantasia. Bowin's load-bearing positive thesis is that this capacity does not presuppose counting (arithmein) or intellect (nous). Anchored in Phys. 4.11.219a3-4, 219a30-b1; Mem. 1.449b29, 450a19, 451a17.

concepts.label: Intellectual cognition / measurement of time
concepts.summary: Apprehending time by a measure (gnōrizein metrō) — counting determinate units of time (days, hours). Requires sortal concepts, hence nous. Anchored in Mem. 2.452b7-8, 452b30-453a4; Phys. 4.14.223b13-24.

concepts.label: The now (nun)
concepts.summary: Aristotle's now is the instantaneous limit between past and future motion stages — perfectly and actually indivisible qua instantaneous (Phys. 4.13.222a14). Bowin's reading: the now divides POTENTIALLY (Phys. 4.13) but actually-exists prior to counting (Phys. 8.8.263a27-8). Common sense perceives a plurality of nows without counting them.

concepts.label: Before-and-after (proteron-hysteron) as time-structure
concepts.summary: Time is 'a number of motion in respect of the before and after' (Phys. 4.11.219b1-2). The before/after relation is what is perceived as countable. Bowin reads this as 'a plurality of instantaneous motion stages studied qua indivisible and countable.' The structure is in motion, not laid on it by intellect.

concepts.label: Memory–time-perception circularity
concepts.summary: Memory presupposes the perception of time (Mem. 1.449b28-29), and the perception of motion (hence time) seems to presuppose memory (past stages must be remembered). Bowin's resolution: the circularity is interdefinitional, not vicious; both are co-grounded in phantasmata.

concepts.label: Phantasma in De Memoria
concepts.summary: Two phantasmata: one of the event remembered, one of the time elapsed (Mem. 2.452b31-453a4). Phantasmata are individuated particulars (Mem. 1.450a27-32 signet-ring; Mem. 2.452b23 ff.). Phantasmata are raw material for the intellect's grasp of essences (Mem. 1.449b31-450a7). The phantasma of a past event AS past is the structural condition of perceiving time.

concepts.label: Counting (arithmein) vs measuring (metrein)
concepts.summary: Counting is the type of measurement most exact because the measure (the unit) is absolutely indivisible (Metaph. I.1.1053a1, 23). Strictly, only nows may be counted (absolutely indivisible). Durations are MEASURED — 'a number of a sort' (tis arithmos, Phys. 4.12.220a27-8). At Phys. 4.14.223b13-24 the verb arithmein is used in the extended sense of measuring.

concepts.label: Determinate (hōrismenon) vs indeterminate (aoriston) time
concepts.summary: Pseudo-Philoponus's distinction (Philoponus 1897, 580.27-37). Determinate time is a time used as a measure because marked out by regular motion (e.g., a day, hour). Indeterminate time is the residue without sortal marking. Determinate-time perception is the work of deliberative phantasia; indeterminate-time perception is the work of perceptual phantasia.

concepts.label: Deliberative phantasia
concepts.summary: DA 3.11.434a6-15: in beings capable of calculating, deliberative phantasia synthesizes many phantasmata into a single unified phantasma. Bowin reads this as the mechanism producing the normalized image of a day, the unified phantasma usable as a measure. Contrasted with perceptual phantasia (DA 3.11.434a5-6), found in all animals. Builds on Plato Prot. 356d-e metrētikē technē as background.

concepts.label: Perceptual phantasia
concepts.summary: Found in all animals (DA 3.11.434a5-6; DA 2.3.415a6-11; DA 3.3.428a10 ff.; Metaph. Α.1.980b25-7). Underlies animal perception of time as indeterminate. Sufficient for perceiving motion stages and the before-and-after relation.

concepts.label: Common sense (koinē aisthēsis) and perception of number
concepts.summary: DA 3.1.425a16 + DA 2.6.418a7-11: the common sense, in animals and humans, perceives common sensibles including number directly. Bowin's load-bearing claim: perceiving 'three nows' does not require counting them. Animal sortless numerical competence ('subitizing,' fn. 20 to Nieder 2005) corroborates.

concepts.label: Incidental perception
concepts.summary: DA 2.6.418a16-17: incidental perceptibles include 'where' and 'what.' Cashdollar 1973 reading (fn. 15): incidental perception does not require sortal concepts. Caston 1996 p. 42 (fn. 16): right that incidental sensibles may involve cooperation of intellect in humans, but it is not essential. Underwrites the claim that perceiving nows as individuals does not require sortal concept-possession.

concepts.label: Mind-dependence of time (Phys. 4.14)
concepts.summary: Phys. 4.14.223a21-29: 'no soul, no time, except there could be what underlies time' — motion. Bowin's reading: in the absence of nous, time would not be MEASURABLE (countable in the extended sense), but motion's before-and-after would still obtain. Not a logical error (contra Mignucci 1987 pp. 184-186; modality confusion contra Sorabji 1983 p. 89 ff.) but a modest claim about the measurability relation.

concepts.label: Measurable-by-measure instrumental relation
concepts.summary: Metaph. Δ.15: measurables/knowables/visibles are relatives, called such not because they are of something else but because something else (the measure) is OF them. Cats. 7.6b28-36: 'the measurable is measurable BY the measure' (instrumental dative). The measure is only incidentally related to the measurable's measurability. Phys. 4.14.223b13-15: time is counted by some determinate time.

concepts.label: Memory and recollection (mnēmē, anamnēsis)
concepts.summary: Memory is a state or affection of perception when time passes (hotan genētai chronos, Mem. 1.449b25). It is an active engagement that involves perceiving in addition (prosaisthanetai, Mem. 1.450a19) that one perceived/heard/learned this before. Recollection is described as a syllogismos tis (Mem. 2.453a5-13). Mnēmonikoi are distinguished from anamnēstikoi (fn. 38: Top. 8.14.163b28; Mem. 2.452a12; Insomn. 1.458b20).

concepts.label: Perceiving time having passed vs perceiving time as passing
concepts.summary: Bowin's distinction (§3): Aristotle in Phys. 4.11 speaks of perceiving time HAVING PASSED (gegonenai chronos, perfect tense), not perceiving time AS PASSING (the specious-present-style continuous awareness). The seven temporal-passage references in Phys. 4.11 are about passage as a metaphysical phenomenon, not perception of it.

concepts.label: Specious present (rejected)
concepts.summary: James 1905 vol. 1 p. 631 'short duration of which we are immediately and incessantly sensible.' Sorabji 2004 p. 91 tentatively detects this at Mem. 1.451a31 (aorist epathe). Bowin: uncorroborated elsewhere in Aristotle; little evidence for the concept.

concepts.label: Sortal concepts and the genus-of-measure constraint
concepts.summary: Mem. 2.452b30-453a4: the measure must be of the same genus as what it measures. Spatial magnitudes are measured by spatial magnitudes; times by some definite time. Measuring requires the universal sortal concept of the measure-unit. Hence measuring time requires sortal concepts (day, hour) and so nous. Perceiving without sortal concepts is available to animals.

concepts.label: Non-conceptual perceptual content
concepts.summary: Bowin's fn. 39 + main text §4: while the disambiguating sortal concept of 'day' may guide deliberative phantasia in producing a normalized image, the resulting phenomenal content can remain non-conceptual (citing Tye 1995 pp. 140-141 on faces-vase figures and ambiguous decompositions). Empeiria in animals may be non-conceptual (NE 7.3.1147b5).

concepts.label: Synthesis of phantasmata (Post. An. 2.19 / Metaph. Α.1)
concepts.summary: Post. An. 2.19.100a3-9: 'from perception there comes memory, and from many memories of the same thing experience.' Metaph. Α.1.980b26-981a12: 'many memories of the same thing produce finally the capacity for a single experience.' Bowin reads deliberative phantasia (DA 3.3.427b18-20) as the active analog of this synthesis, generating a unified image from multiple phantasmata.

concepts.label: Time and circular motion (Phys. 4.14)
concepts.summary: Phys. 4.14.223b13-24: 'uniform circular motion is most of all a measure, because the number of this is most easily known.' Time is thought to be the motion of the celestial sphere — the other motions are measured by this one, and time by this motion. Background for the measure-of-time as celestial-rotation-tracked.

readings.label: Anti-mathematization of Phys. 4.11
readings.summary: Reading that 'number' in 'time is a number of motion in respect of the before and after' (Phys. 4.11.219b1-2) refers to a perceptible plurality of instantaneous motion stages, NOT to an act of counting requiring nous. Yields: perceiving time is perceiving a number of nows directly, available to the common sense. Bowin's positive reading. Contests Albert the Great (Alberti Magni 1890 p. 100), Themistius (1899 120.12-17), Coope 2005, and Sorabji 1983.

readings.label: Non-vicious phantasma circularity
readings.summary: Reading of Mem. 1.450a19-22 + Mem. 2.452b31-453a4 such that memory and perception of time are interdefined through phantasmata: two phantasmata, one for event, one for time elapsed. The circularity is non-vicious because 'perceiving time' and 'remembering an event' are the same activity under different descriptions. Bowin's positive reading; contests Sorabji's broader-sense-of-perceive reading (fn. 25).

readings.label: Determinate-time-via-deliberative-phantasia reading of Pseudo-Philoponus
readings.summary: Reading that Pseudo-Philoponus (Philoponus 1897, 580.27-37) distinguishes perception of determinate vs indeterminate time as a distinction in PHENOMENAL CONTENT, mediated by deliberative phantasia's synthesis-of-images. Animals: indeterminate (seasonal) time. Humans: determinate time (days, hours) because deliberative phantasia produces the normalized day-image. Contests Polansky 2007 p. 530 and Moss 2012 p. 146 (deliberative phantasia individuated only by USE).

readings.label: Phys. 4.14 'no soul, no time' as measurability-not-existence claim
readings.summary: Reading that Phys. 4.14.223a21-29 means: in the absence of nous, motion's before-and-after still obtains; only the MEASURABILITY of time fails (no measure stands in measuring relation). Routed through Metaph. Δ.15 + Cats. 7.6b28-36 instrumental dative of measure. Contests Mignucci 1987 pp. 184-186 (logical error reading) and Sorabji 1983 p. 89 ff. (modality confusion reading).

readings.label: Counting-plays-a-small-role reading of Phys. 4.10-14
readings.summary: Reading that arithmein in Phys. 4.10-14 plays a much smaller role than commentators have supposed (fn. 18-19 to Coope 2005, Sorabji 1983). Only 3 of 8 post-219b1-2 occurrences of arithmein concern counting itself; 3 concern the count-vs-countable distinction; 2 are idiosyncratic (extended-sense measurement). Counting is reserved for measurement; perception of time-as-countable does not require it.

tensions.label: Memory presupposes time-perception, but time-perception (via motion) seems to presuppose memory
tensions.summary: If to perceive motion is to perceive a plurality of motion stages, and only one stage is present at a time, past stages must be remembered. So perception of motion (and time) seems to presuppose memory. But Aristotle says memory presupposes the perception of time (Mem. 1.449b28-29). Bowin's resolution: the circularity is interdefinitional. Perceiving time and remembering an event are the same activity under different descriptions, both mediated by phantasmata. The circle is non-vicious because the perception of time does NOT, strictly, presuppose memory — only that one currently has phantasmata of past phases AS past. Sites: §3 (centerpiece).

tensions.label: Time depends on nous (Phys. 4.14) vs animals perceive time (Mem. 1)
tensions.summary: Phys. 4.14.223a21-29 says 'if no soul, no time' — apparently making time depend on rational counters. Mem. 1 (450a14-20) credits animals (who lack nous and so cannot count) with memory, which presupposes the perception of time. Resolution: Phys. 4.14 means time is not MEASURABLE without nous (no measure stands in measuring relation); motion's before-and-after still obtains. Sites: introduction + §5.

tensions.label: Counting brings nows into existence (Coope-style) vs nows exist potentially prior to counting (Bowin)
tensions.summary: Coope 2005 reads Phys. 4.11 as making the act of counting/marking-off constitutive of the existence of nows. Bowin contests using Phys. 4.13.222a14 (the now divides potentially) and Phys. 8.8.263a27-8, 263b3-6 (time has infinitely many potential parts) — nows exist potentially prior to any act of counting, and even if marking-off is required, it can be perceptual discrimination, not counting. Sites: §1, fn. 12, 18, 42.

tensions.label: Sorabji's broader-sense-of-perceive reading vs Bowin's same-activity reading
tensions.summary: Sorabji 2004 reads Mem. 1.450a19-22 (prosaisthanetai) as Aristotle using 'perceive' in a broader sense to emphasize that memory is a perceptual, not intellectual, activity. Bowin reads more strictly: Aristotle calls this perceiving-time because he does not distinguish remembering-time from perceiving-time-as-passing — the two are the same activity under different descriptions. Sites: §3, fn. 25.

tensions.label: Polansky/Moss's use-individuation of deliberative phantasia vs Bowin's content-individuation
tensions.summary: Polansky 2007 p. 530 and Moss 2012 p. 146 hold deliberative phantasia is distinguished from perceptual phantasia only by what it is USED FOR. Bowin contends there is a difference in phenomenal content: the active manipulation of images by intellect (the synthesis-of-phantasmata into a unified day-image) produces a different kind of phantasmal output. Sites: §4 + fn. 37.

tensions.label: Mathematical objects: bringing-to-actuality vs already-actual in time case
tensions.summary: Aristotle elsewhere talks of geometers bringing geometric objects to actuality through proof-construction (Metaph. Θ.1.1051a21-33). This suggests grasping mathematical objects requires abstraction and so intellect. Bowin maintains the time case is different: instantaneous motion stages are perfectly and actually indivisible qua instantaneous; no abstraction is required. Sites: §1, fn. 7.
